title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: The social worker has 2 court days to file papers after your child is removed.
source_says: shall be released within 48 hours after having been taken into custody ... excluding nonjudicial days ... unless within said period of time a petition ... has been filed
steps: Searched 'WIC 313 released within 48 hours excluding nonjudicial days petition filed'; opened the leginfo page for section 313 and read subdivision (a). 48 hours not counting non-court days matches '2 court days'.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: The first hearing is the next court day.
source_says: not later than the expiration of the next judicial day after a petition
steps: Searched 'WIC 315 detention hearing next judicial day after petition filed'; opened public.law section 315. The next judicial day runs from the filing of the petition.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Weekends and holidays do not count
source_says: excluding nonjudicial days
steps: Opened leginfo section 313 and read subdivision (a).

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: If your child was removed, it must be held within 15 court days of the detention order.
source_says: the petition must be set for hearing within 15 judicial days ... from the date of the order of the court directing such detention
steps: Searched 'WIC 334 jurisdiction hearing within 15 judicial days detention order 30 calendar days'; opened leginfo section 334.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: If your child was not removed, within 30 days of the petition
source_says: Upon the filing of the petition, the clerk of the juvenile court shall set the same for hearing within 30 days
steps: Opened leginfo section 334.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Must be held within 60 days of the detention hearing
source_says: longer than 60 days ... after the hearing at which the minor was ordered removed or detained ... unless the court finds that there are exceptional circumstances requiring a continuance
steps: Searched 'WIC 352 continuance dispositional hearing 60 days exceptional circumstances six months'; opened public.law 352(b) and 358(a). 60 days is a cap on delays, not the normal date. 358(a) says a delay for a detained child 'shall not exceed 10 judicial days' after the jurisdiction finding. 352(b) lets the judge go past 60 days for 'exceptional circumstances' but never 'more than six months' after the detention hearing. The public.law page also shows a 30 day limit for an Indian child.
fix: If your child was removed, the disposition hearing is usually held within 10 court days after the jurisdiction hearing. Delays should not push it past 60 days after the detention hearing. A judge can go past 60 days only for very unusual reasons, and never past 6 months.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Held about 6 months after the disposition hearing, and no later than 12 months after the child entered foster care
source_says: held 6 months after the initial dispositional hearing ... no later than 12 months after the date the child entered foster care ... whichever occurs earlier
steps: Searched 'WIC 366.21 six months after the initial dispositional hearing'; opened public.law 366.21 and read (e)(1).

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Judge reviews progress on case plan
source_says: The extent of progress that has been made toward alleviating or mitigating the causes necessitating placement in foster care.
steps: Searched 'WIC 366 status of every dependent child reviewed no less frequently than once every six months'; opened public.law 366 and read (a)(1).

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Held approximately 12 months after the child entered foster care
source_says: The permanency hearing shall be held no later than 12 months after the date the child entered foster care.
steps: Opened public.law 366.21 and read (f)(1). The law says 'no later than' 12 months, which fits 'approximately'.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Critical hearing where judge may set a WIC § 366.26 hearing if reunification is not progressing
source_says: Order that a hearing be held within 120 days, pursuant to Section 366.26
steps: Opened public.law 366.21 and read subdivision (g), the options when the child is not returned at the permanency hearing.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: If services were extended, held around 18 months
source_says: the permanency review hearing shall occur within 18 months after the date the child was originally removed from the physical custody of their parent or legal guardian.
steps: Searched 'WIC 366.22 permanency review hearing within 18 months'; opened public.law 366.22 and read (a)(1). The 18 months count from the day the child was first removed.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Last chance for reunification in most cases
source_says: the court may continue the case for up to six months for a subsequent permanency review hearing ... provided that the hearing shall occur within 24 months
steps: Opened public.law 366.22. (a)(3) says if the child is not returned the court 'shall order that a hearing be held' under 366.26. (b)(1) allows more time only for listed groups (parents in residential drug treatment, minor or nonminor dependent parents, parents just out of custody), so 'in most cases' matches.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Must be held within 120 days of the order setting the hearing
source_says: The hearing shall be held no later than 120 days from the date of the permanency review hearing.
steps: Opened public.law 366.21(g)(4) ('Order that a hearing be held within 120 days, pursuant to Section 366.26') and 366.22(a)(3).

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: The first hearing (detention) happens within a few court days.
source_says: not later than the expiration of the next judicial day after a petition
steps: Opened leginfo 313 (48 hours not counting non-court days to file) and public.law 315 (hearing the next court day after filing).

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: The social worker has 2 court days to file papers, and the hearing is the next court day.
source_says: shall be released within 48 hours after having been taken into custody ... excluding nonjudicial days
steps: Opened leginfo 313 and public.law 315 ('not later than the expiration of the next judicial day after a petition').

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: The jurisdiction hearing is within 15 court days, about 3 weeks, if your child was removed.
source_says: the petition must be set for hearing within 15 judicial days
steps: Opened leginfo section 334. 15 court days is 3 weeks of weekdays.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Then you have review hearings every 6 months where the judge checks your progress.
source_says: shall be reviewed periodically as determined by the court but no less frequently than once every six months
steps: Opened public.law 366 and read (a)(1).

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: You usually get about one year to complete your case plan, or only 6 months if your child is under 3, and get your kids back.
source_says: court-ordered services shall be provided for a period of 6 months from the dispositional hearing ... but no longer than 12 months from the date the child entered foster care
steps: Searched 'WIC 361.5 child under three court-ordered services six months'; opened public.law 361.5. (a)(1)(A) for a child 3 or older: services 'ending 12 months after the date the child entered foster care'. (a)(3) allows extension 'not to exceed 18 months'. Note the 6 months counts from the disposition hearing.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Judge decides if child can return home or must stay in foster care during the case
source_says: The court shall order the release of the child from custody unless a prima facie showing has been made
steps: Opened public.law 319 (returned by search 'WIC 319 initial petition hearing') and read subdivision (c)(1).

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Judge determines if the allegations are true
source_name: Judicial Council booklet, Juvenile Dependency Court and You, p. 9
source_says: If the judge decides the allegations are true, the court will take authority over your child.
steps: Searched for the Judicial Council booklet on courts.ca.gov, opened the PDF, read the jurisdiction hearing part on p. 9.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: and if the child should be declared a dependent
steps: Two sources I opened do not line up. The booklet p. 9 says that if the allegations are true 'then your child will become a dependent of the court' at the jurisdiction stage. WIC 360 (public.law) puts this at disposition: 'After receiving and considering the evidence on the proper disposition of the case' the court 'may order and adjudge the child to be a dependent child of the court.' I could not open WIC 356 (leginfo page failed). Recorded both, so COULD_NOT_VERIFY.
fix: At the jurisdiction hearing the judge decides if what the petition says is true. If it is true, the court takes authority over your child. The formal dependency order is made at the disposition hearing.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Can be combined with jurisdiction hearing or held separately
source_says: Sometimes the dispositional hearing happens at the same time as jurisdiction.
steps: Opened the booklet PDF and read the disposition part on p. 9. WIC 358(a) (public.law) also allows a short delay between the two.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: Judge decides case plan, services, and placement
source_says: the judge will decide what you should do to make things better for your family and your child.
steps: Opened the booklet p. 9 and public.law WIC 358: 'the court shall hear evidence on the question of the proper disposition' and the report 'shall include the individual child's case plan'.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
statement: If reunification fails, this hearing establishes a permanent plan (adoption, guardianship, or long-term foster care)
source_says: Order that the child be permanently placed with a fit and willing relative ... Order that the child remain in foster care
steps: Opened public.law 366.26 and read subdivision (b). The section does not use the words 'long-term foster care'. Its list is: adoption, tribal customary adoption, relative guardianship, nonrelative guardianship, placement with a fit and willing relative, or remaining in foster care. 'another planned permanent living arrangement' is only for a child '16 years of age or older, or a nonminor dependent'. I tried to open SB 794 (2015) on leginfo to confirm when the term changed but the page failed, so I did not mark this OUT_OF_DATE.
fix: If reunification fails, this hearing sets a permanent plan. The choices are adoption, tribal customary adoption, guardianship, living with a fit and willing relative, or staying in foster care with a plan.

title: Timeline for Court Hearings
source_says: not later than the expiration of the next judicial day after a petition
steps: The cited sections support most of the page. But four facts on the page come from sections that are not cited: the next-court-day hearing is WIC 315, the 60 day limit is WIC 352(b), the 12 month and 6 month service periods are WIC 361.5(a)(1), and reviews every 6 months are WIC 366(a)(1). I opened each on public.law.

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: Welfare and Institutions Code Section 300 establishes the grounds for juvenile court dependency jurisdiction. A child may be adjudged a dependent of the court under various subdivisions
source_says: within the jurisdiction of the juvenile court which may adjudge that person to be a dependent child of the court
steps: Searched 'WIC 300 child within jurisdiction of juvenile court subdivisions (a) through (j)'; opened public.law section 300 and read the opening words.

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: (a) serious physical harm inflicted by parent/guardian
source_says: serious physical harm inflicted nonaccidentally upon the child
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (a).

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: (b) neglect or failure to protect
source_says: The failure or inability of the child’s parent or guardian to adequately supervise or protect the child.
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (b)(1)(A) to (D). (b)(1) also needs 'serious physical harm or illness' or a substantial risk of it.

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: (c) serious emotional damage
source_says: The child is suffering serious emotional damage, or is at substantial risk of suffering serious emotional damage
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (c).

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: (d) sexual abuse
source_says: The child has been sexually abused ... or there is a substantial risk that the child will be sexually abused
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (d).

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: (e) severe physical abuse of child under 5
source_says: The child is under five years of age and has suffered severe physical abuse by a parent
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (e).

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: (f) caused death of another child through abuse/neglect
source_says: The child’s parent or guardian caused the death of another child through abuse or neglect.
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (f).

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: (g) child left without care or support
source_says: The child has been left without any provision for support
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (g).

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: (h) child freed for adoption
source_says: The child has been freed for adoption by one or both parents for 12 months
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (h). The law adds a 12 month condition the short label leaves out.

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: (i) cruelty
source_says: The child has been subjected to an act or acts of cruelty by the parent or guardian
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (i).

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: (j) a brother or sister was abused or neglected and this child is at risk.
source_says: The child’s sibling has been abused or neglected ... there is a substantial risk that the child will be abused or neglected
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (j).

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: This law lists the reasons a child can be placed under court protection. It includes physical abuse, neglect (not providing proper care), sexual abuse, emotional harm
source_says: A child who comes within any of the following descriptions is within the jurisdiction of the juvenile court
steps: Opened public.law section 300 and read (a) through (d).

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: and situations where a parent cannot care for a child because of drug or alcohol problems.
source_says: The child has suffered, or there is a substantial risk that the child will suffer, serious physical harm or illness, as a result of any of the following
steps: Opened public.law section 300 and read (b)(1) and (b)(1)(D): 'The inability of the parent or guardian to provide regular care for the child due to the parent's or guardian's mental illness, developmental disability, or substance abuse.' The simple line drops the condition that the child was seriously hurt or sick, or is at substantial risk of that.
fix: and cases where a child was badly hurt or sick, or is at serious risk of that, because a parent cannot give regular care due to drug or alcohol problems.

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: 300(a) - Physical Harm: Serious physical harm inflicted nonaccidentally by parent/guardian
source_says: serious physical harm inflicted nonaccidentally upon the child
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (a).

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: 300(b) - Neglect: Failure to protect, supervise, or provide necessities
source_says: The willful or negligent failure of the parent or guardian to provide the child with adequate food, clothing, shelter, or medical treatment.
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (b)(1)(A) through (D).

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: 300(c) - Emotional Damage: Serious emotional damage from conduct of parent
source_says: as a result of the conduct of the parent or guardian or who has no parent or guardian capable of providing appropriate care.
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (c). The law also covers a child with no parent able to give the right care.

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: 300(d) - Sexual Abuse: Child has been sexually abused
source_says: The child has been sexually abused
steps: Opened public.law section 300, read (d). The law also covers substantial risk of sexual abuse.

title: WIC Section 300 - Dependency Jurisdiction
statement: WIC §300
source_says: A child who comes within any of the following descriptions is within the jurisdiction of the juvenile court
steps: The citation is the section the page describes. Opened it on public.law. The page's external link is the leginfo page for section 300, which the search also returned; I read the public.law copy.

title: WIC Section 388 - Request to Change Orders
statement: Allows any party to ask the court to change orders based on changed circumstances.
source_says: Any parent or other person having an interest in a child who is a dependent child ... upon grounds of change of circumstance or new evidence, petition the court
steps: Searched 'WIC 388 any parent or other person having an interest petition change of circumstance or new evidence'; opened public.law 388 and read (a)(1). New evidence is a second ground.

title: WIC Section 388 - Request to Change Orders
statement: WIC Section 388 permits any person having an interest in a dependent child to petition the court for a hearing to change, modify, or set aside any order of court previously made.
source_says: for a hearing to change, modify, or set aside any order of court previously made or to terminate the jurisdiction of the court.
steps: Opened public.law 388, read (a)(1).

title: WIC Section 388 - Request to Change Orders
statement: The petitioner must show: (1) new evidence or changed circumstances, AND (2) that the proposed change would be in the child's best interest.
source_name: Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.570(d); WIC 388(a)(1), (d)
source_says: fails to state a change of circumstance or new evidence ... fails to show that the requested modification would promote the best interest of the child
steps: Opened rule 5.570 from the Title Five index on courts.ca.gov and read (d), (e), (h). Also public.law 388(d): 'If it appears that the best interests of the child ... may be promoted ... the court shall order that a hearing be held'.

title: WIC Section 388 - Request to Change Orders
statement: This law lets you ask the judge to change a court order if your situation has changed.
source_says: upon grounds of change of circumstance or new evidence, petition the court
steps: Opened public.law 388, read (a)(1). The law also allows a request based on new evidence.

title: WIC Section 388 - Request to Change Orders
statement: You file a form (JV-180) explaining what has changed and why the change would be good for your child.
source_says: must be made on form Request to Change Court Order (form JV-180).
steps: Opened rule 5.570 on courts.ca.gov and read (b). The selfhelp.courts.ca.gov forms page also lists JV-180 as 'Request to Change Court Order'.

title: WIC Section 388 - Request to Change Orders
statement: If you make a good case, the judge will hold a hearing.
source_name: Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.570(d), (f); WIC 388(d)
source_says: order that a hearing on the petition be held within 30 calendar days after the petition is filed
steps: Opened rule 5.570. (d) lets the court deny without a hearing only if the petition fails to state a change or new evidence or fails to show best interest. (f) then requires a hearing or a hearing on whether to have one.

title: WIC Section 388 - Request to Change Orders
statement: Requirements: Must show changed circumstances AND best interest of child
source_says: upon grounds of change of circumstance or new evidence, petition the court
steps: Opened public.law 388(a)(1) and rule 5.570(d). The law gives two ways in: a change of circumstance or new evidence. This line names only one, so a parent with new evidence could think they cannot file.
fix: Must show changed circumstances or new evidence, AND that the change is best for the child

title: WIC Section 388 - Request to Change Orders
statement: Process: File JV-180 form; court may grant hearing or deny if no prima facie showing
source_says: fails to state a change of circumstance or new evidence that may require a change of order
steps: Opened rule 5.570. (b) names form JV-180. (d) allows denial without a hearing when the petition does not make the needed showing. (a) says the petition 'must be liberally construed in favor of its sufficiency.'

title: WIC Section 388 - Request to Change Orders
statement: WIC §388
source_says: Any parent or other person having an interest in a child who is a dependent child of the juvenile court
steps: The cited section is the one the page describes. Opened it on public.law. The JV-180 form comes from rule 5.570(b), which the page does not cite.

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: Dependency hearings are closed to the public.
source_name: WIC 346; Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.530(e)
source_says: the public shall not be admitted to a juvenile court hearing.
steps: Opened public.law section 346 and rule 5.530 on courts.ca.gov ('Except as provided below, the public must not be admitted to a juvenile court hearing.').

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: The judge, commissioner, or referee, who runs the hearing and decides
steps: WIC 346 (public.law) names 'The judge or referee'. The Judicial Council booklet only says 'the judge'. Neither page I opened uses the word 'commissioner', and the shared search limit for this run was used up before I could look for a source on commissioners. Judge and referee are confirmed; only 'commissioner' is unverified.
fix: No change needed if a source for commissioners is added on a later check.

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: The child.
source_name: Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.530(b)(1); WIC 349(a)
source_says: The child or nonminor dependent;
steps: Opened rule 5.530 from the Title Five index on courts.ca.gov and read the (b) list. Also public.law 349(a): the minor 'is entitled to be present at the hearing.'

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: Children 10 and older must be told about the hearing and asked if they want to come.
source_says: the court shall determine whether the minor ... was properly notified of their right to attend the hearing and inquire whether the minor ... was given an opportunity to attend.
steps: Opened public.law section 349 and read (d). If the child was not told or wanted to come and could not, the court must delay the hearing unless that is not in the child's best interest.

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: The parents and any legal guardian
source_says: All parents, de facto parents, Indian custodians, and guardians of the child
steps: Opened rule 5.530, read (b)(2).

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: De facto parents and, in cases under the Indian Child Welfare Act, an Indian custodian and a representative of the tribe
source_says: In a proceeding described by rule 5.480, a representative of the Indian child's tribe;
steps: Opened rule 5.530, read (b)(2) ('All parents, de facto parents, Indian custodians, and guardians of the child') and (b)(7).

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: The lawyers: yours, the other parent's, the child's, and county counsel for the agency
source_says: the county counsel or district attorney must appear and represent the petitioner
steps: Opened rule 5.530. (b)(3): 'Counsel representing the child or the parent, de facto parent, guardian, adult relative'. (d) covers county counsel in section 300 cases.

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: The social worker
source_says: The probation officer or social worker;
steps: Opened rule 5.530, read (b)(4).

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: A CASA volunteer, if the child has one
source_says: Any CASA volunteer;
steps: Opened rule 5.530, read (b)(6).

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: The court clerk, the court reporter, and sometimes a bailiff
source_says: The court clerk; ... The official court reporter, as provided in rule 5.532; ... At the court's discretion, a bailiff; and
steps: Opened rule 5.530, read (b)(8), (9), (10).

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: The public can come in only if a parent asks and the child agrees.
source_says: Unless requested by a parent or guardian and consented to or requested by the minor concerning whom the petition has been filed, the public shall not be admitted
steps: Opened public.law 346. Rule 5.530(e) says the same and adds that 'the court may permit others to be present', so it is still up to the judge.

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: The judge can also let in a person who has a direct and real interest in the case.
source_says: The judge or referee may nevertheless admit such persons as he deems to have a direct and legitimate interest in the particular case or the work of the court.
steps: Opened public.law 346. Rule 5.530(e) repeats it.

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: Court is private. Only people who are part of the case can be in the room, unless the judge says yes to someone else.
source_says: Except as provided below, the public must not be admitted to a juvenile court hearing.
steps: Opened rule 5.530 and public.law 346.

title: Who Is in the Courtroom
statement: Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.530; WIC §§346, 349
source_says: Any other persons entitled to notice of the hearing under sections 290.1 and 290.2.
steps: Opened all three. Rule 5.530(b) has the list of people, 346 has the public rule, 349(d) has the age 10 rule. The page's link (www.courts.ca.gov/cms/rules/index/five/rule5_530) is the same page I opened without the www.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: It is a written document
source_says: A written case plan shall be completed within a maximum of 60 days
steps: Searched 'WIC 16501.1 case plan written'; opened public.law 16501.1 and read (e).

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: Specific services you must complete (parenting classes, therapy, drug treatment, etc.)
source_says: The case plan shall identify specific goals and the appropriateness of the planned services in meeting those goals.
steps: Opened public.law 16501.1, read (g)(2). The examples in brackets are examples only.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: Visitation schedule with your children
source_says: the frequency of contact between the natural parents or legal guardians and the child shall be specified in the case plan.
steps: Opened public.law 16501.1, read (g)(5)(A).

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: Goals you must achieve (stable housing, employment, sobriety, etc.)
source_says: The case plan shall identify specific goals
steps: Opened public.law 16501.1, read (g)(2). The examples in brackets are examples only.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: Timeline for completion
source_says: They are in your case plan. Talk to your social worker to make sure you understand what to do, how, and by when.
steps: Opened the booklet PDF, glossary p. 28.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: Completing your case plan is the key to reunification
source_says: Do everything in your case plan, even if you do not agree.
steps: Opened the booklet PDF p. 24. The booklet does not promise return; it says doing the plan matters most.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: The judge will review your progress at every hearing
source_says: The extent of progress that has been made toward alleviating or mitigating the causes necessitating placement in foster care.
steps: Opened public.law 366(a)(1), the list of what the court decides at each review. 16501.1(g)(14) adds 'The case plan shall be included in the court report, and shall be considered by the court'.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: Your compliance affects whether your children come home
source_says: the judge will probably keep control over your child longer and may not allow your child to go back home.
steps: Opened the booklet PDF p. 24, what happens if you do not follow the plan.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: Failure to comply can result in termination of your parental rights
source_name: Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.695(g)(2); Judicial Council booklet pp. 13, 25
source_says: Notify the parents that their parental rights may be terminated if custody is not returned within 6 months
steps: Opened rule 5.695 from the Title Five index. Also booklet p. 25: 'the court will make a permanent plan for your child, and your child may be taken from you forever'. Booklet p. 13 adds 'Termination of services is NOT the same as termination of parental rights.' So 'can result' is right; it is not automatic.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: You can object to services through your attorney
source_says: call your lawyer as soon as possible and go to the court date
steps: Opened booklet p. 23 (what to do if you disagree with the report, which holds the case plan). public.law 16501.1(g)(12)(A): 'Whenever possible, parents and legal guardians shall participate in the development of the case plan.'

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: You can request modifications if circumstances change
source_says: upon grounds of change of circumstance or new evidence, petition the court
steps: Opened public.law 388, read (a)(1).

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: Stay in regular contact with your social worker ... Keep your attorney informed of your progress
source_says: Keep in touch with your attorney.
steps: Opened booklet p. 23, which also says to 'keep in touch with him or her, too' about the social worker.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: Maintain consistent visitation with your children
source_says: If your child was taken from your home, it's very important to visit your child.
steps: Opened booklet p. 24.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: Your case plan is a list of things you must do to get your children back - like parenting classes, therapy, or drug testing.
source_says: These are called reunification requirements and are put in your case plan.
steps: Opened booklet p. 10.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: You need to complete everything on your case plan, go to all your appointments, and visit your kids regularly.
source_says: Do everything in your case plan, even if you do not agree.
steps: Opened booklet p. 24.

title: Understanding the Case Plan
statement: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 358
source_says: shall include the individual child's case plan developed pursuant to Section 16501.1.
steps: Opened public.law 358. It only says the social worker's report must include the case plan. What a case plan holds (goals, services, visits, parent taking part, getting a copy) is in WIC 16501.1, which I opened and which the page does not cite.
fix: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 16501.1 (what a case plan is); § 358(b) (the plan goes in the court report); § 388 (asking for changes)

title: What Happens at Detention Hearing
statement: The detention hearing is the first court appearance after a child is removed from home.
source_says: not later than the expiration of the next judicial day after a petition
steps: Opened public.law 315: a child taken into custody and not released gets a detention hearing the next court day after the petition.

title: What Happens at Detention Hearing
statement: (1) Appoint attorneys for parents who need one.
source_says: The court must appoint counsel for any parent or guardian unable to afford counsel

title: When the Case Closes: Dismissal and Exit Orders
statement: If your child will live with one parent and the parents are not together, the judge makes exit orders when closing the case.
source_name: Judicial Council booklet p. 29; WIC 362.4(a); Judicial Council pamphlet 'What happens after your dependency case is dismissed?'
steps: Sources I opened do not agree on whether this always happens. Booklet p. 29: 'If your case is dismissed when your child is living with you and not with the child's other parent, the judge will make an exit order.' WIC 362.4(a) (public.law): the court 'may issue ... an order determining the custody of, or visitation with, the child'. The Judicial Council pamphlet on dismissal: 'Sometimes, when a dependency case is dismissed, a judge makes a custody order'. Recorded all three, so COULD_NOT_VERIFY.
fix: If your child will live with one parent and the parents are not together, the judge can make exit orders when closing the case. Ask your lawyer if the judge will make one in your case.

WIC 319 (public.law) has no visitation language. Booklet p. 8: 'the judge will make orders about when and where you can visit your child.'

steps: Search returned law.cornell.edu 25 U.S.C. 1903; opened it and read paragraph (4). Booklet p. 30: 'It applies to your family only if your child is a member of an Indian tribe or is eligible for membership because you or the child's other parent is a member' and 'only tribes can decide if your child is an Indian child.' Heritage alone is not the test.
fix: ICWA protections: These apply if your child is a member of an Indian tribe, or can be a member and has a birth parent who is a member. Only the tribe decides this. Tell the judge and your lawyer right away about any tribal ties so they can check.
